checks.rationale: Without `aaa new-model`, the device falls back to line-level passwords and cannot use TACACS+/RADIUS, per-command authorization or accounting at all. It is the prerequisite for every other AAA control in this catalogue.
subject: aaa new-model
checks.title: `aaa new-model` not enabled

checks.rationale: Without an explicit login method list, interactive access falls back to whatever the line itself defines (often nothing, or a shared line password), which defeats per-user accountability entirely.
remediation: aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
subject: aaa authentication login
checks.title: No `aaa authentication login` method list

checks.rationale: If the only authentication method is a remote TACACS+/RADIUS group and that service becomes unreachable, nobody can log in to the switch at all, including to fix the outage. A `local` fallback keeps the device recoverable.
remediation: aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
subject: aaa authentication login
checks.title: Login method list has no local fallback

checks.rationale: Without this line, privileged-mode access is gated only by the shared `enable secret`, so there is no per-user record of who escalated to privilege 15.
remediation: aaa authentication enable default group tacacs+ enable
subject: aaa authentication enable default
checks.title: `aaa authentication enable default` absent

checks.rationale: Without exec authorization, any account that authenticates successfully gets an interactive shell at whatever privilege the line grants, regardless of what the AAA server says that user is entitled to.
remediation: aaa authorization exec default group tacacs+ local
subject: aaa authorization exec
checks.title: `aaa authorization exec` absent

checks.rationale: By default IOS does not apply exec/command authorization to the console line even when `aaa authorization exec` is configured elsewhere; `aaa authorization console` is what extends the same policy to console sessions.
subject: aaa authorization console
checks.title: `aaa authorization console` absent

checks.rationale: Without command accounting at privilege 15, there is no audit trail of what a privileged administrator actually typed, which matters both for incident response and for change-control review.
remediation: aaa accounting commands 15 default start-stop group tacacs+
subject: aaa accounting commands
checks.title: `aaa accounting commands` absent for privilege 15

checks.rationale: A single authentication server is a single point of failure: if it is unreachable and there is no local fallback in use, administrative access to the switch is lost along with it. Two independent servers keep AAA available through a single outage.
subject: tacacs server
radius server
checks.title: Fewer than two TACACS+/RADIUS servers configured

checks.rationale: A method list that references a `group` name with no matching `aaa group server` definition silently falls through to the next method in the list — often nothing — so the intended authentication path never actually runs.
subject: aaa authentication
aaa authorization
aaa accounting
checks.title: AAA method list names an undefined server group

checks.rationale: Type 0 stores the password in clear text in the configuration and type 7 uses a Cisco proprietary cipher that public tools reverse in milliseconds. A privilege-15 account protected this way is effectively unprotected against anyone who can read the running configuration.
subject: username
checks.title: Local user at privilege 15 with a type 0 or type 7 password

checks.rationale: `enable-password` stores its value with the same reversible cipher as type-7 passwords, and type-5 MD5-crypt secrets are crackable offline at commodity speed. `enable-secret` with a type-8/9 (PBKDF2/scrypt) hash is the only form that resists offline attack.
subject: enable password
enable secret
checks.title: `enable-password` present, or `enable-secret` uses type 5 or weaker

checks.rationale: Without this line, every type-0 secret already present in the configuration (or added later by a script or template) is stored and displayed in clear text rather than the weak-but-obscured type-7 form.
subject: service password-encryption
checks.title: `service password-encryption` not enabled

checks.rationale: DHCP snooping is the prerequisite for Dynamic ARP Inspection and IP Source Guard alike; without it enabled globally, a rogue DHCP server anywhere on the access layer can hand out addresses, gateways and DNS servers of its choosing to any client.
subject: ip dhcp snooping
checks.title: `ip dhcp snooping` not enabled globally

checks.rationale: Globally enabling snooping without naming any VLANs leaves every VLAN unprotected in practice, since the feature only inspects traffic on the VLANs explicitly listed.
subject: ip dhcp snooping vlan
checks.title: DHCP snooping enabled but no VLAN list

checks.rationale: A VLAN carrying end-host traffic that is missing from the snooping VLAN list gets none of the rogue-server protection the feature is meant to provide on exactly the segment where end hosts request addresses.
subject: ip dhcp snooping vlan
switchport access vlan
checks.title: An access VLAN is not covered by the snooping VLAN list

checks.rationale: Every port is untrusted by default once snooping is enabled, including the uplink toward the real DHCP server; without marking that uplink trusted, legitimate DHCP server replies arriving on it are dropped and clients cannot get addresses at all.
subject: ip dhcp snooping trust
checks.title: `ip dhcp snooping trust` missing on an uplink

checks.rationale: Without a rate limit, a single misbehaving or malicious host can flood DHCP messages fast enough to consume CPU on the snooping process, affecting every other port on the switch.
subject: ip dhcp snooping limit rate
checks.title: `ip dhcp snooping limit rate` not set on access ports

checks.rationale: Without a persistent bindings database, every DHCP snooping and IP Source Guard binding is lost on reload, leaving legitimate hosts without confirmed IP-to-port bindings until each one renews its lease.
subject: ip dhcp snooping database
checks.title: `ip dhcp snooping database` not configured

checks.rationale: Option 82 insertion on an untrusted port that a downstream relay or switch also inserts into can cause the switch to drop the double-tagged packet outright unless `allow-untrusted` is explicitly reasoned about, silently breaking DHCP for hosts behind that device.
remediation: Confirm whether any untrusted port faces a relay that also inserts option 82, and set `ip dhcp snooping information option allow-untrusted` there if so.
subject: ip dhcp snooping information option
checks.title: `ip dhcp snooping information option` left enabled without `allow-untrusted` handling

checks.rationale: Without DAI, ARP spoofing within a VLAN is unopposed even though DHCP snooping is already tracking legitimate IP-to-MAC bindings; DAI is what actually uses that data to reject forged ARP replies.
subject: ip arp inspection vlan
checks.title: Dynamic ARP Inspection not enabled on snooped VLANs

checks.rationale: Without the additional `validate` checks, DAI only confirms the IP-to-MAC binding itself and not that the Ethernet and ARP header MACs agree, and a trusted port set on an access-facing interface exempts exactly the traffic DAI exists to inspect.
remediation: ip arp inspection validate src-mac dst-mac ip
subject: ip arp inspection validate
ip arp inspection trust
checks.title: DAI `validate src-mac dst-mac ip` not configured, or trust misplaced

checks.rationale: Hard-coding speed or duplex on one end of a link while the other end auto-negotiates is a classic cause of a duplex mismatch, which shows up as slow, intermittently-lossy traffic that is disproportionately hard to diagnose compared to how simple the fix is.
subject: speed
duplex
checks.title: Hard-coded `speed` or `duplex` on a copper access port

checks.rationale: An undocumented trunk or uplink forces whoever is troubleshooting a topology issue months or years later to reverse-engineer what the other end of the link is from CDP/LLDP or physical tracing instead of reading it directly off the interface.
subject: description
checks.title: Trunk or uplink has no `description`

checks.rationale: Proxy ARP lets the switch answer ARP requests on behalf of hosts on a different subnet, which can be abused to redirect traffic through the device and also leaks internal topology information to anything on the local segment.
subject: ip proxy-arp
checks.title: `ip proxy-arp` not disabled on a routed interface

checks.rationale: ICMP redirects and unreachables both hand an off-path attacker information about the network's routing and addressing, and redirects specifically can be used to alter a host's forwarding path without the host's administrator ever touching its routing table.
subject: ip redirects
ip unreachables
checks.title: `ip redirects` / `ip unreachables` not disabled on a routed interface

checks.rationale: Directed broadcast forwarding lets a packet sent to a subnet's broadcast address from outside that subnet be flooded to every host on it, historically the mechanism behind smurf-style amplification attacks.
subject: ip directed-broadcast
checks.title: `ip directed-broadcast` enabled

checks.rationale: Without unicast RPF, the switch will happily forward a packet whose source address could not have arrived via the interface it actually came in on, which is exactly the spoofed-source traffic pattern used in reflection and amplification attacks.
remediation: ip verify unicast source reachable-via rx
subject: ip verify unicast source
checks.title: `ip verify unicast source reachable-via rx` absent on a routed edge

checks.notes: Does not fire when any interface carries `switchport voice vlan`; see CSC-IFC-0008, which covers that case instead.
checks.rationale: CDP announces the device's platform, IOS version and hostname to anything on the connected segment, which is reconnaissance value handed to an attacker for free on any port that does not specifically need CDP for phone provisioning.
subject: cdp run
checks.title: CDP left enabled globally

checks.notes: Fires instead of CSC-IFC-0007 when voice VLANs are present; the correct posture is per-interface `no cdp enable` on non-voice ports, not a global `no cdp run`.
checks.rationale: Cisco IP phones use CDP (or LLDP-MED) to learn their voice VLAN and power negotiation parameters from the switch; disabling CDP globally on a switch that also serves voice ports breaks phone provisioning rather than just reducing reconnaissance exposure.
subject: switchport voice vlan
cdp enable
checks.title: CDP disabled on a switch carrying `switchport voice vlan`

checks.rationale: VLAN 1 carries untagged control-plane traffic (CDP, VTP, PAgP/LACP) by default across every trunk on the network; leaving it as the native VLAN makes VLAN-hopping via double tagging trivial and mixes management-adjacent traffic with an ID every device assumes is present.
subject: switchport trunk native vlan
checks.title: Native VLAN on a trunk is VLAN 1

checks.rationale: If the trunk's native VLAN matches a VLAN also assigned to access ports elsewhere, double-tagged frames only need to be tagged with the outer native VLAN and the inner target VLAN to hop between them, since the native VLAN's tag is stripped on egress.
subject: switchport trunk native vlan
switchport access vlan
checks.title: Native VLAN equals an access VLAN in use

checks.rationale: VLAN 1 is the default for every unconfigured port and every trunk's native VLAN, so an end host placed there shares a broadcast domain with any device an installer forgot to assign, plus whatever control-plane traffic rides untagged on VLAN 1 trunks nearby.
subject: switchport access vlan
checks.title: Access port assigned to VLAN 1

checks.rationale: An active VLAN1 SVI gives the switch a management-reachable IP address on the same broadcast domain every unconfigured port defaults into, which is exactly the segment an attacker plugging into an unused jack lands on.
subject: interface Vlan1
checks.title: `interface Vlan1` not shut down

checks.rationale: Carrying every VLAN across every trunk means a new VLAN added anywhere in the network propagates to links that never needed it, and a compromised access switch can reach broadcast domains it has no legitimate traffic for.
subject: switchport trunk allowed vlan
checks.title: Trunk allowed-VLAN list is `all` rather than explicit

checks.rationale: With DTP still negotiating, an attacker who connects a device configured to speak DTP can potentially convince the switch port to become a trunk, gaining access to every VLAN the trunk is allowed to carry.
subject: switchport nonegotiate
checks.title: DTP not disabled (`switchport nonegotiate` absent on a trunk)

checks.rationale: A port with no explicit mode defaults to `dynamic auto` or `dynamic desirable`, both of which will negotiate into trunk mode if the far end asks; setting an explicit access/trunk mode removes that ambiguity entirely.
subject: switchport mode
checks.title: Port left at DTP dynamic (no explicit `switchport mode`)

checks.rationale: An unused but active port is a physical entry point to the network for anyone who can reach the wiring closet or a patch panel, with none of the port-security or VLAN controls a provisioned port would have.
subject: shutdown
checks.title: Unused port not shut down

checks.rationale: Even a shut-down port retains its assigned VLAN in the configuration; leaving it on a production VLAN means the moment someone re-enables it (intentionally or by mistake) it lands directly on live user traffic instead of an isolated blackhole VLAN.
subject: switchport access vlan
checks.title: Unused port not parked in an unused VLAN

checks.rationale: Without port security, any number of MAC addresses can appear behind an access port, which allows an attacker to attach an unmanaged switch or hub and multiply the number of devices with access through that single jack.
subject: switchport port-security
checks.title: Port security not configured on an access port

checks.rationale: A high MAC maximum defeats much of the point of port security on a single-host access port, and a `protect` violation mode silently drops offending traffic without logging or disabling the port, leaving the event unnoticed.
subject: switchport port-security maximum
switchport port-security violation
checks.title: Port security `maximum` above 3, or violation mode not restrict/shutdown

checks.rationale: Without storm control, a broadcast storm from a misbehaving NIC, a bridging loop, or a malicious host can consume the port's and the switch's forwarding capacity, degrading service for every other port sharing the same ASIC or backplane resource.
subject: storm-control
checks.title: Storm control not configured on an access port

checks.rationale: In server or client mode, any switch that joins the VTP domain with a higher revision number can silently overwrite every switch's VLAN database, including deleting VLANs still in active use — a well-documented cause of network-wide outages.
subject: vtp mode
checks.title: VTP mode is server or client rather than transparent/off

checks.rationale: An unauthenticated VTP domain accepts VLAN database updates from any switch that joins it with the same domain name, which is exactly the mechanism CSC-L2-0013 warns about; a password at minimum requires an attacker to know it before injecting an update.
subject: vtp password
checks.title: VTP domain configured without a VTP password

checks.rationale: With no remote syslog destination, the only record of events is the local buffer, which is lost on reload and is also the first thing an attacker with configuration access would clear to cover their tracks.
subject: logging host
checks.title: No `logging host` configured

checks.rationale: A single syslog server is a single point of failure for the device's entire audit trail; if it is down during an incident, nothing sent during that window is recoverable.
subject: logging host
checks.title: Fewer than two syslog destinations

checks.rationale: A trap level coarser than `informational` (6) drops routine but security-relevant events — interface state changes, ACL denies, login successes and failures — before they ever reach the syslog server.
subject: logging trap
checks.title: `logging trap` level below `informational`

checks.rationale: Log entries without a full, timezone-qualified timestamp are difficult to correlate against other systems during an investigation, especially across daylight-saving transitions or when servers and network gear are not in the same timezone.
remediation: service timestamps log datetime msec localtime show-timezone
subject: service timestamps log
checks.title: `service timestamps log datetime msec localtime show-timezone` absent

checks.rationale: A small local buffer wraps within minutes on a busy switch, so by the time an operator opens a session to investigate, the events that would explain what happened have already been overwritten.
subject: logging buffered
checks.title: `logging buffered` absent or below 16 KB

checks.rationale: Without a fixed source interface, the address a syslog message appears to come from can change with the active uplink or routing table, which breaks source-address filtering and per-device grouping on the log-collection side.
subject: logging source-interface
checks.title: `logging source-interface` not set to a stable interface

checks.rationale: Without configuration-change logging, there is no record of who changed what and when on the device itself; the archive feature timestamps and attributes each change as it happens.
subject: archive
log config
checks.title: `archive` / `log config` not enabled

checks.rationale: Without `hidekeys`, the change-logging archive stores the literal secret values typed during a configuration change, which turns an audit feature into a second place secrets leak from.
subject: log config
hidekeys
checks.title: `archive log config` missing `hidekeys`

checks.rationale: Console logging at `debugging` can flood an active terminal session with output during a busy period, to the point that typed commands are hard to see and CPU spent formatting console messages competes with the operator's own troubleshooting.
subject: logging console
checks.title: `logging console` left enabled at a verbose level

checks.rationale: The HTTP management server transmits configuration and credential material without encryption and has a long history of unauthenticated remote-code-execution advisories. A switch that only needs SSH and console access gains nothing from also listening on TCP/80, so the service should stay off unless a specific integration requires it.
subject: ip http server
checks.title: HTTP server enabled (`ip http server`)

checks.rationale: Even TLS-protected web management should not be reachable from arbitrary source addresses: an access-class scopes the listener to the management subnet so a compromised host elsewhere on the network cannot reach the device's configuration UI.
subject: ip http secure-server
ip http access-class
checks.title: HTTPS server not restricted by `ip http access-class`

checks.rationale: Running the plaintext HTTP listener without also enabling the TLS listener means any web-based management session is fully readable on the wire. If web management is needed at all, the encrypted form should be the one in use.
subject: ip http secure-server
checks.title: `ip http secure-server` disabled while `ip http server` is enabled

checks.rationale: PAD (X.25 Packet Assembler/Disassembler) support is a legacy service with no role on a modern campus switch. Leaving it enabled adds an unused listener and code path to the attack surface for no operational benefit.
subject: service pad
checks.title: `service pad` enabled

checks.rationale: The small servers (echo, chargen, discard, daytime) are diagnostic holdovers that can be abused for reflection and amplification traffic. They are not needed for normal switch operation and should stay disabled.
subject: service tcp-small-servers
service udp-small-servers
checks.title: TCP/UDP small servers enabled

checks.rationale: The BOOTP server lets the switch answer legacy boot-image requests from the network, a function a campus access/distribution switch never performs. An enabled BOOTP responder is one more unauthenticated service reachable from any attached segment.
subject: ip bootp server
checks.title: `ip bootp server` enabled

checks.rationale: Finger discloses logged-in user information to any unauthenticated requester, which is reconnaissance value handed to an attacker for free. There is no operational reason to run it on a production switch.
subject: ip finger
service finger
checks.title: `ip finger` / `service finger` enabled

checks.rationale: Source-routed packets let the sender dictate the forwarding path, which can be used to bypass topology-based access controls and to probe internal addressing. Modern networks have no legitimate use for it on a switch's management or routed interfaces.
subject: ip source-route
checks.title: `ip source-route` enabled

checks.rationale: Autoloading configuration from a network TFTP server on boot lets anyone who can spoof that server (or intercept the boot-time broadcast) push an arbitrary configuration onto the device. Startup configuration should come only from local NVRAM.
subject: service config
checks.title: `service config` (network autoload) enabled

checks.rationale: The Smart Install client listens on TCP/4786 with no authentication and has been used in the wild to pull running configuration, push a replacement startup-config, or reload the device outright. Unless the switch is an active Smart Install director-managed client, the feature should be off.
subject: vstack
checks.title: `vstack` (Smart Install client) not disabled

checks.rationale: Call Home transmits inventory, crash and diagnostic data off-box to Cisco (or a configured destination). On a network where outbound telemetry is not wanted, or where the destination has not been reviewed, the feature should stay disabled.
subject: service call-home
call-home
checks.title: `service call-home` enabled (phones home to Cisco)

checks.rationale: NETCONF and RESTCONF are full programmatic configuration channels; enabling either without a control-plane or interface ACL means any host that can reach the management address can attempt to manage the switch, not merely observe it.
remediation: Restrict management access with a control-plane ACL or `ip http access-class` before enabling `restconf`/`netconf-yang`.
subject: netconf-yang
restconf
checks.title: `netconf-yang` or `restconf` enabled without an access restriction

checks.rationale: With DNS lookups enabled but no resolver configured, every mistyped command at the CLI triggers a lookup that has to time out before the prompt returns, which is a well-known operator annoyance that also slows down scripted configuration.
subject: ip domain-lookup
ip name-server
checks.title: `ip domain-lookup` enabled with no `ip name-server`

checks.notes: Generic referential check; the engine excludes any (kind, name) pair already reported by CSC-VTY-0003, CSC-SNMP-0005, CSC-NTP-0005 or CSC-AAA-0009.
checks.rationale: A command that names an ACL, server group or similar object which is never defined elsewhere in the configuration has no effect at all: IOS silently treats the reference as a no-op rather than rejecting the line, so the intended control is not applied.

subject: access-class
ip access-group
aaa group server
checks.title: Configuration references an undefined object

checks.rationale: Without an external time source, the switch's clock drifts freely, which breaks certificate validity checks, log correlation and any time-based ACL or scheduling feature in use.

checks.title: No `ntp server` configured

checks.rationale: A single time source cannot be cross-checked for sanity by the NTP algorithm and is a single point of failure for the device's clock if that source becomes unreachable or starts serving bad time.
subject: ntp server
checks.title: Fewer than two NTP sources

checks.rationale: Without authentication, the switch accepts time updates from any host that can reach it on UDP/123, which lets an attacker skew the clock to undermine certificate validation and confuse log timelines.
subject: ntp authenticate
checks.title: `ntp authenticate` not enabled

checks.rationale: An `ntp server` line with no `key` clause accepts unauthenticated time from that peer even when `ntp authenticate` is globally enabled, which quietly defeats the authentication for that specific source.

checks.title: An `ntp server` has no `key` binding

checks.rationale: A key id referenced by a server line but never marked trusted is never actually used to validate that peer's packets, so the association behaves as if authentication were off for it.

checks.title: An `ntp server ... key N` has no matching `ntp trusted-key N`

checks.rationale: MD5 is cryptographically broken for collision resistance and is markedly weaker than the SHA1/SHA2 options IOS also supports for the same command; a stronger algorithm costs nothing extra to configure.
subject: ntp authentication-key
checks.title: NTP authentication key uses MD5 rather than SHA1/SHA2

checks.rationale: Without a fixed source interface, the address NTP packets originate from can change with the active uplink, which breaks any authentication-key or ACL scoping keyed to a specific source address on the server side.
subject: ntp source
checks.title: `ntp source` not set to a stable interface

checks.rationale: Without an explicit boot list, the device falls back to whatever image ROMMON finds first, which after a flash reorganization or a partially completed upgrade may not be the image the operator believes is running.
subject: boot system
checks.title: No `boot system` statement, or a non-deterministic boot order

checks.rationale: A network boot source (TFTP/FTP/HTTP) means the device's boot image depends on that server being reachable and trustworthy at every reload; anyone who can spoof or compromise it can hand the switch an arbitrary image at boot time.
subject: boot system
checks.title: `boot system` names an image over a network URL

checks.rationale: Without automatic recovery, a port err-disabled by BPDU Guard, UDLD or a security violation stays down until an operator manually notices and re-enables it, turning a transient event into an extended outage for whatever was connected.

checks.title: `errdisable recovery cause` not configured for the common causes

checks.rationale: A very short recovery interval can re-enable a port into the same fault condition repeatedly before the underlying issue clears, generating a flap loop instead of giving the condition time to resolve.

checks.title: `errdisable recovery interval` below 300 seconds

checks.rationale: `switch N priority P` is set in privileged EXEC mode, not configuration mode, and is stored outside the running-config, so a static audit can see from other `switch N ...` lines that a stack exists but cannot see, let alone judge, the priority actually assigned to any member.
remediation:
Operator step, run in privileged EXEC on the stack (this is not a configuration-mode command and is never stored in running-config): `switch priority

` for each member, then confirm with `show switch`.

checks.title: Stack member priority cannot be verified from a config file (`switch N priority`)

checks.rationale: This check applies only to stacked systems. Without a persistent stack MAC, losing the original master member changes the stack's system MAC address, which can re-trigger DHCP on every downstream device that keys off the gateway's MAC and can break certain licensing or ACL rules bound to it.

checks.title: Stack MAC persistence not configured (`stack-mac persistent timer`)

checks.rationale: Without SSO, a control-plane failover on redundant supervisor/stack hardware causes a full reload of the data plane instead of a stateful switchover, turning a supervisor fault into a full outage rather than a brief interruption.
subject: redundancy
mode sso
checks.title: `redundancy mode sso` absent on a stack-capable platform

checks.rationale: The default device-tracking probe interval and count can generate enough ARP probe traffic on a large access-layer deployment to be mistaken for a duplicate-IP condition or to add measurable load; tuning the probe parameters is a common but easy to overlook step after enabling the security features that depend on it.
subject: ip device tracking
checks.title: `ip device tracking` probe defaults left in place (duplicate-IP symptoms)

checks.rationale: SNMPv1/v2c authenticate with a community string sent in clear text and offer no message integrity or encryption at all; anyone who can see the traffic can read or, for an RW community, rewrite the device's configuration.
remediation: Remove the SNMPv1/v2c community-string configuration and migrate to SNMPv3 with `auth priv`.
subject: snmp-server community
checks.title: SNMPv1/v2c community string configured

checks.rationale: A read-write community lets anyone who obtains it push configuration changes over SNMP, which combined with the protocol's lack of encryption makes an RW v1/v2c community one of the fastest routes to full device compromise.
remediation: Remove the RW community; use SNMPv3 with a per-user `priv` credential instead.
subject: snmp-server community
checks.title: Community string is read-write (`RW`)

checks.rationale: Strings like `public` and `private` are the first values any scanner tries; a community that matches a well-known default is equivalent to having no authentication at all.
remediation: Remove the default-named community and issue a unique, non-guessable value, or migrate to SNMPv3.
subject: snmp-server community
checks.title: Community string matches a known default

checks.rationale: Without an ACL clause, an SNMPv1/v2c community is valid from any source address that can reach the device, not just the network-management station it was issued for.
subject: snmp-server community
checks.title: Community string not restricted by an ACL

checks.rationale: If the ACL a community string names does not exist, IOS applies no restriction at all, so the community is reachable from anywhere despite appearing to be scoped.
subject: snmp-server community
checks.title: Community ACL is referenced but undefined

checks.rationale: Without a `priv`-level v3 group, SNMP traffic is either unauthenticated, authenticated-but-unencrypted, or falls back to v1/v2c entirely — none of which meets the confidentiality bar for a management protocol carrying device state.
subject: snmp-server group
checks.title: No SNMPv3 group with `priv` configured

checks.rationale: A trap/inform destination configured for v1/v2c sends the community string in every notification, so even a device otherwise locked down to SNMPv3 for polling can still leak a usable credential through its outbound traps.

checks.title: A configured SNMP trap/inform target uses v1/v2c instead of SNMPv3

checks.rationale: Without traps enabled for link state, configuration changes and authentication failures, the network-management station has no push notification of these events and depends entirely on polling to notice them, which is slower and easy to under-scope.

checks.title: No `snmp-server enable traps` for link/config/auth events

checks.rationale: Without persistence, interface index numbers can be reassigned across a reload, which silently breaks any NMS dashboard, threshold or automation keyed on ifIndex until it is manually re-mapped.
subject: snmp ifmib ifindex persist
checks.title: `snmp ifmib ifindex persist` not configured

checks.rationale: IOS never echoes SNMPv3 user credentials or their auth/priv algorithm choice back into `show running-config`, so a static audit can confirm which v3 groups exist but cannot verify user-level hygiene; that requires an interactive `show snmp user` on the device.
remediation: Run `show snmp user` on the device and confirm each user's auth/priv algorithms and group membership match policy.
subject: snmp-server user
checks.title: SNMPv3 user inventory cannot be audited from a running-config

checks.rationale: SSHv1 has known cryptographic weaknesses (including a CRC-32 integrity flaw) that were fixed by the SSHv2 redesign; leaving version negotiation open lets an older or downgrade-capable client fall back to the weaker protocol.

checks.title: `ip ssh version 2` not enforced

checks.rationale: SSH cannot start at all without a host key, and generating one requires `ip domain-name` to already be set; a switch missing either prerequisite falls back to an unencrypted management transport by default without an obvious error to the operator.

ip domain-name
checks.title: No RSA/EC key generated (`crypto key` / `ip domain-name` prerequisites absent)

checks.rationale: A Diffie-Hellman modulus below 2048 bits is within reach of well-resourced offline attacks against the key-exchange, weakening the confidentiality the SSH session is supposed to provide.

checks.title: `ip ssh dh min size` below 2048

checks.rationale: CBC-mode ciphers are vulnerable to padding-oracle style attacks against SSH and have been superseded by AEAD/CTR modes; restricting the offered cipher list to modern algorithms removes the weaker options from ever being negotiated.

checks.rationale: HMAC-MD5 and, to a lesser extent, HMAC-SHA1 offer weaker collision resistance than the SHA2-based MAC options IOS also supports, so permitting them widens the set of algorithms an attacker can try to downgrade a session to.
remediation: ip ssh server algorithm mac hmac-sha2-256 hmac-sha2-512
subject: ip ssh server algorithm mac
checks.title: `ip ssh server algorithm mac` permits HMAC-SHA1 or MD5

checks.rationale: The 1024-bit group-1 exchange is considered breakable by a sufficiently resourced attacker, and group-14-sha1 pairs an adequate group with an outdated hash; restricting to group-14-sha256 or group-exchange forms avoids both weaknesses.
remediation: ip ssh server algorithm kex diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256
subject: ip ssh server algorithm kex
checks.title: `ip ssh server algorithm kex` permits a group-1/group-14-sha1 exchange

checks.rationale: A high retry count gives a password-guessing attempt more tries per connection before the session is dropped, which is a small but free improvement to close.

checks.rationale: A long negotiation timeout lets a client hold open a half-established SSH session longer than necessary, which is a minor but easily avoided contributor to session-table exhaustion under a connection flood.

checks.rationale: A running-config audit can see that a trustpoint exists and enumerate its declared enrollment method, but it cannot validate certificate chain trust or expiry from configuration text alone; that requires an interactive `show crypto pki certificate` on the device.

checks.rationale: Legacy PVST converges on the order of 30-50 seconds per topology change, while Rapid-PVST/MST converge in roughly a second on a well-designed topology; on a campus network that difference is the gap between a link flap being invisible and being an outage.

checks.rationale: Without PortFast, an access port runs the full listening/learning cycle every time an end host's NIC comes up, delaying DHCP and adding tens of seconds to boot-time network availability for no protective benefit on a port with no other switch attached.
subject: spanning-tree portfast
checks.title: PortFast not enabled on access ports

checks.rationale: A PortFast port skips STP's normal loop-detection states, so if someone plugs in a switch or hub instead of an end host, BPDU Guard is what shuts the port down before a loop can form; without it enabled by default, every individual PortFast port must be protected by hand.
subject: spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default
checks.title: BPDU Guard is not enabled by default on PortFast ports

checks.rationale: A PortFast port with BPDU Guard explicitly disabled (or never inherited) will keep forwarding if a rogue switch is attached, letting that switch participate in the spanning-tree topology and potentially become root.
subject: spanning-tree bpduguard
checks.title: BPDU Guard missing on an individual access port

checks.rationale: Without Root Guard, a misconfigured or rogue switch attached downstream that advertises a superior BPDU can become the new root bridge for the whole topology, pulling traffic paths through a device never intended to carry them.
subject: spanning-tree guard root
checks.title: Root Guard absent on ports facing another switch

checks.rationale: Loop Guard prevents a port from transitioning to forwarding when it stops receiving BPDUs due to a unidirectional link failure rather than an actual topology change, which is exactly the failure mode that otherwise causes an undetected bridging loop.
subject: spanning-tree loopguard default
checks.title: Loop Guard not enabled by default

checks.rationale: BPDU filtering stops the port from sending or processing BPDUs at all, which removes STP's loop-detection on that port entirely rather than merely adjusting timers; a loop formed through a filtered port will not be caught by spanning tree.
subject: spanning-tree bpdufilter
checks.title: `spanning-tree bpdufilter` enabled (hides loops)

checks.rationale: Leaving root election to the default priority means the root bridge is whichever switch happens to have the lowest MAC address, which can silently become an access switch with no uplink capacity to be the network's root.

checks.rationale: A single switch's configuration only shows its own claimed priority, not the priorities advertised by its neighbors, so whether it is actually well-placed as root or secondary root for a VLAN can only be judged by comparing configurations across the topology.
remediation: Compare `spanning-tree vlan <x> root primary/secondary` placement across all switches in the topology, not from a single device's configuration.

checks.title: Root bridge placement cannot be judged from one config

checks.rationale: A unidirectional fibre or copper link failure can leave a port's link light up while traffic only flows one way, which spanning tree alone cannot always detect; UDLD aggressive mode err-disables such a port before it causes a loop or black-holed traffic.
